Cormorant
KOR-mo-rant
noun
From the Old French cormaran, from the Latin corvus marinus, “sea-raven”; a large diving sea-fowl of proverbial greediness, rendering Hebrew names of birds that haunt water and ruins.

Biblical Definition

The cormorant is a great diving sea-fowl, black and long-necked, so given to swallowing fish that its name became a byword for greed. The law forbids it to Israel’s table: “And the little owl, and the cormorant, and the great owl” (Lev 11:17), and again, “And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant” (Deu 14:17). Two things mark nearly every fowl on that list — they live by taking life, and they haunt places of death and waste. The cormorant is both a hunter and a squatter in ruins: “But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it” (Isa 34:11); “both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it” (Zep 2:14). The point of the prohibition was never dietetics. It was a daily, edible lesson in separation. Three times a day Israel handled the difference between what God had marked off and what He had not, and the reason given is never hygiene but holiness: “Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean… And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine” (Lev 20:25–26). The bird was a schoolmaster. It taught a nation that the line between clean and unclean is drawn by God, and that a severed people eats differently because it belongs differently.

Webster 1828 Definition

A large voracious sea-fowl of the diving kind; forbidden as food to Israel and a tenant of ruined cities.

expand to see more

CORMORANT, a large web-footed fowl of the pelican kind, remarkable for its voracity.

From Old French cormaran, Latin corvus marinus, “sea-raven.”

Figuratively, a glutton; one insatiable in appetite.

Reckoned among the unclean fowls (Lev 11:17; Deu 14:17).

Named with the bittern as possessor of desolated places (Isa 34:11).

Key Scripture

Lev 11:17 — "And the little owl, and the cormorant, and the great owl,"

Deu 14:17 — "And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant,"

Isa 34:11 — "But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness."

Lev 20:26 — "And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine."

Modern Corruption

The clean-and-unclean law is dismissed as primitive food superstition; Scripture gives it as the daily catechism of a severed people.

expand to see more

The common corruption is to explain the unclean-bird list away as ancient sanitation — a pre-modern people fumbling toward food safety and calling it religion. Scripture never gives that reason. The reason it gives is the character of God and the status of His people: I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people, that ye should be mine. Reduce the law to hygiene and you have explained the letter while destroying the point. The prohibition was not medicine; it was a boundary marker worn at every meal, so that a nation could not eat a mouthful without remembering that it had been marked off for God and could not live like the nations around it.

The fulfilment is not the abolition of the principle but the arrival of the substance. Christ, declaring the heart to be the seat of defilement, purged all meats (Mar 7:19); Peter on the housetop was told, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Act 10:15); and Paul writes that “every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4). The dividing wall between Jew and Gentile is down, and the cormorant is not the church’s problem. But the separation the bird taught did not die with the bird — it changed its object. The old line ran between kinds of meat; the new line runs between the world and the holy, and it is drawn just as sharply: “come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing” (2Co 6:17).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The sea-raven — a voracious diving fowl, unclean under the law, tenant of ruins in the oracles.

expand to see more

Cormorant — Old French cormaran, Latin corvus marinus, “sea-raven.”

Its proverbial greed made the name a byword for the glutton.

Forbidden to Israel among the unclean fowls (Lev 11:17; Deu 14:17).

It possesses Idumea and lodges in Nineveh’s lintels (Isa 34:11; Zep 2:14).

The prohibition taught separation, not sanitation (Lev 20:25–26).

Usage

"The cormorant was forbidden not because it was unwholesome but because Israel was severed."

"A cormorant in the lintels is the sign that a city has been handed over."

"The clean-and-unclean table was a catechism a nation ate three times a day."
